original_question: Is every infinite almost radically closed field ample, where almost radically closed means that for every positive integer n the subgroup of n-th powers has finite index in K^times?
target_in_paper: The open problem in Section 6, "Radically closed fields": Is every infinite radically closed field ample?
correct_elements: Your draft correctly identifies that the target is an open problem about ample fields, it keeps the ambient object as an infinite field K, and it uses the multiplicative-group viewpoint on root-taking via subgroups of K^\times. It also asks the right yes/no type of question.
missing_details: The paper's official target is about radically closed fields, not the weaker-looking 'almost radically closed' variant in your draft.

To match the paper faithfully, the hypothesis should be stated in the standard radical-closure form: for every n >= 1, every element of K^\times is an n-th power in K^\times; equivalently, K^\times is divisible.
The question should explicitly say that K is a field and that K is infinite.
To be stand-alone, the term 'ample' should be defined; in the paper's background this is one of the standard equivalent notions of a large field.
Using only the finite-index condition [K^\times : (K^\times)^n] < \infty changes the strength and scope of the hypothesis away from the section title and official terminology of the paper.
The notation (K^\times)^n should be identified as the subgroup of n-th powers in K^\times if that notation is used.
refined_question: Let K be an infinite field. Assume that K is radically closed, meaning that for every integer n >= 1 the multiplicative group K^\times is n-divisible (equivalently, every a in K^\times has an n-th root in K, or K^\times = (K^\times)^n for all n >= 1). Must K be ample, i.e. a large field in the sense that every smooth K-curve with a K-rational point has infinitely many K-rational points?
justification: Your draft is clearly aiming at the problem isolated in the paper's Section 6, whose title is explicitly "Radically closed fields". That makes the nearest paper-faithful target the radically closed version, not a broader finite-index weakening. The paper's earlier background section supplies the needed meaning of 'ample', so the refined question should include that definition to be fully stand-alone. The table of contents shows Section 6 begins on page 7, while the introduction and background begin on pages 1 and 2 respectively, which are the natural places for the open-problem framing and the definition of ample fields.
